content: Barium carbonate (BaCO3), also referred to as witherite, is a chemical compound that has applications in the production of rat poison, bricks, and cement. Witherite crystallizes in the orthorhombic crystal system. The crystals are almost always twinned in groups of three, which results in pseudo-hexagonal forms that bear some resemblance to bipyramidal quartz crystals. The crystal faces are typically rough and exhibit horizontal striations. The mineral was named after William Withering, who, in 1784, identified it as chemically distinct from barytes (barium sulfate). Witherite is found in lead ore veins in various locations, including Hexham in Northumberland, Alston in Cumbria, and Anglezarke near Chorley in Lancashire, as well as a few other sites. It is prone to alteration into barium sulfate when exposed to water containing dissolved calcium sulfate. As a result, witherite crystals are often coated with a layer of barytes. Witherite serves as the primary source of barium salts and is mined extensively in Northumberland. It is utilized in the production of rat poison, glass, and porcelain. Historically, it was also employed in the sugar refining process. Additionally, it is used to regulate the chromate-to-sulfate ratio in chromium electroplating baths. Barium carbonate reacts with a variety of acids to form soluble barium salts, such as barium chloride. However, its reaction with sulfuric acid is limited due to the formation of barium sulfate, which is highly insoluble.
